extracted.intended_audience: readers and editors of Scottish ballads; literary scholars and folklorists
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing, editing, and annotating traditional Scottish ballads and related material with historical, linguistic, and comparative-mythological commentary. Emphasis on preserving original texts while providing explanatory notes and cross-references for modern readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of poetry and tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: In a work, avowedly dedicated to the preservation of the poetry and tradition of the 'olden time,' it would be unpardonable to omit this opportunity...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the original poems and ballads are preserved in text and form; prioritize retention of traditional wording, metres, and melodies where available as the core purpose of the volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include observations on popular superstition (Fairies/Elves)
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be unpardonable to omit this opportunity of making some observations upon so interesting an article of the popular creed, as that concerning the Elves, or Fairies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a dedicated discussion of relevant beliefs (origin, attributes, habits) when presenting ballads that invoke or depend on such superstition; treat the topic as integral to understanding the ballads' cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace origins of names and primary ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The intermixture of tribes, of languages, and religion, which has occurred in Europe, renders it difficult to trace the origin of the names which have been bestowed upon such spirits, and the primary ideas which were entertained concerning their manners and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undertake etymological and historical tracing of key terms and concepts (e.g., elf, fairy), acknowledging complexity from linguistic and cultural contact; cite relevant linguistic sources and historical parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative and historical sources (Scandinavian, Saxon, Low German, Icelandic Sagas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word elf ... is of Gothic origin... From the most early of the Icelandic Sagas, as well as from the Edda itself, we learn the belief of the northern nations in a race of dwarfish spirits...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support interpretations with cross-cultural parallels and primary sources (Edda, Sagas, Torfaeus, local chronicles). Include illustrative myths and saga-examples (e.g., Tyrfing) to illuminate analogous motifs in Scottish tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include illustrative tales and saga examples as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of the elfin sword, Tyrfing, may be the most pleasing illustration of this position... Many such tales are narrated in the Sagas;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote or summarize representative tales from sagas and folklore to exemplify attributes and motifs discussed; use these narratives as comparative evidence rather than mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory footnotes for dialect, obsolete words, and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote A: _Waly!_ an interjection. Footnote B: _Stell'd_--Planted. Footnote C: _How_--Hollow. Footnote D: _Know_--Knoll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gloss dialect words and archaisms inline or in footnotes to aid comprehension. Explain cultural references, banners, colours, and local idioms so readers understand historical meaning and connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply historical annotations linking ballads to events and persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on the Battle of Bothwell-Bridge... The object of Claverhouse's revenge... There were two Gordons of Earlstoun... The son, Alexander Gordon of Earlstoun, I suppose to be the hero of the ballad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate ballads with historical context: battles, leaders, local traditions, and archival sources (Fountainhall, Wilson, Creichton, Guild). Where possible, identify historical figures/events and provide documentary citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference related ballads, poems, and musical items
rubrics_metrics.description: See the ballad, entitled, _Brown Adam._ See the _Gay Goss Hawk._ The Lass of Lochroyan--In this volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate related items elsewhere in the collection or in other sources (ballads, odes, tunes). Use cross-references to help readers follow motifs, variants, and musical/lyrical relations across the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original ballad text and dialect forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ballad text presented with dialect: 'O no, O no!' says Earlstoun, 'For that's the thing that mauna be; For I am sworn to Bothwell Hill...' and orthography such as 'An' 'An waly' 'stell'd'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the original wording, lineation, and dialect spellings (with glosses) rather than modernizing; this preserves metre, rhyme, and regional voice important for literary and folkloric analysis.
